lead: An autoencoder is a network that learns to rebuild its own input. It first squeezes the input x through an encoder q(z|x) into a small latent code z, then a decoder p(x|z) produces a reconstruction x-hat. Training makes x-hat close to x. The narrow middle forces the model to keep the main structure and drop noise. Autoencoders are used for denoising, feature extraction, compression and anomaly detection, and the encoder-decoder pattern is the base of variational autoencoders (VAEs), discussed in 6.3. GANs use an entirely different adversarial training scheme.
prereq: You need: the multilayer perceptron and backpropagation from Unit 1, and optimizers and regularization from Unit 2.

blocks.text: An autoencoder has two functions. The encoder q(z|x) maps an input vector x with n real values to a latent vector z with m values. The decoder p(x|z) maps z back to x-hat, a vector of n values. The network is trained so that x-hat copies x. The code z is the only path between the two sides.

When m < n, the autoencoder is undercomplete. The code is narrower than the input, so the model cannot pass every pixel or feature through. It must learn a compact description that keeps what is needed for reconstruction. When m ≥ n, the autoencoder is overcomplete. A wide code can copy the input, so low loss alone does not prove that z is useful.

The encoder-decoder pattern is larger than autoencoders. In machine translation, an encoder reads a source sentence and a decoder writes the target sentence (see Unit 4). In image segmentation, an encoder downsamples and a decoder upsamples to pixel labels (see Unit 3). An autoencoder is the special case where the target is the input itself.

items: Take a mini-batch of inputs x.
Compute reconstruction loss between x and x-hat.
Backpropagate the loss and update encoder and decoder weights.

blocks.text: The loss depends on the input type. For real values, such as temperatures or pixel intensities scaled to [0,1], use mean squared error.

blocks.where: n is the number of input features; xᵢ is the i-th input value; x̂ᵢ is its reconstruction; the sum runs i = 1 to n.

blocks.text: For binary values, such as black/white pixels or presence/absence bits, use binary cross-entropy.
L_BCE = −Σᵢ [xᵢ log x̂ᵢ + (1 − xᵢ) log(1 − x̂ᵢ)]
blocks.where: xᵢ ∈ {0,1} is the i-th input bit; x̂ᵢ is the predicted probability that bit is 1; add a small ε inside each log to avoid log 0.

blocks.text: A denoising autoencoder adds noise to x before encoding. The noise can be Gaussian noise or random pixel masking. The decoder is trained to output the clean x, not the noisy version. The code must remove the corruption, so it learns robust features. At test time, the same network can clean a noisy input.

A sparse autoencoder adds a penalty to the loss, for example λ Σⱼ |zⱼ|. zⱼ is the j-th code unit and λ ≥ 0 controls penalty strength. A KL penalty can instead keep the average activation of each code unit near a small target ρ. The code stays wide but only a few units fire for each input.

A contractive autoencoder adds ||∂z/∂x||_F², the squared Frobenius norm of the Jacobian. This penalizes a code that changes sharply when x changes slightly. Only a few universities teach this variant in detail. Probabilistic encoders and decoders lead to variational autoencoders in 6.3.

Make the encoder and decoder linear: z = W_e x + b_e and x-hat = W_d z + b_d. W_e has size m×n, W_d has size n×m, b_e has m values, and b_d has n values. With squared error and zero biases, training finds an m-dimensional linear subspace that captures the data. The subspace spanned by the columns of W_d matches the subspace of the top m principal components of the data. The columns of W_d need not equal the PCA eigenvectors; any basis of the same subspace gives the same reconstruction error. This is the link between linear autoencoders and PCA.

The compression ratio is n/m, the input dimension divided by the latent dimension. A 1,000-pixel input with a 32-unit code has ratio 1,000/32 = 31.25:1. The ratio measures size reduction, not information kept. For image editing and inpainting with autoencoders, see 6.6.

figure.caption: A 1,000-pixel input is squeezed to a 32-unit code and rebuilt as a 1,000-pixel output; the narrow middle is the bottleneck.

spec.title: Autoencoder bottleneck
spec.aria: Input x of 1,000 pixels passes through an encoder to a 32-unit latent code z, and a decoder rebuilds a 1,000-pixel x-hat.

examples.question: An autoencoder takes a 1,000-pixel input and uses a 32-unit bottleneck. The encoder has a 1,000×32 weight matrix and 32 biases. The decoder has a 32×1,000 weight matrix and 1,000 biases. Compute the total number of trainable parameters and the compression ratio.
steps: Encoder weight count = input units × latent units = 1,000 × 32 = 32,000.
Decoder weight count = latent units × input units = 32 × 1,000 = 32,000.
Compression ratio = input units / latent units = 1,000 / 32 = 31.25.
examples.answer: The model has 65,032 trainable parameters, and the compression ratio is 31.25:1.
examples.check:
n = 1000
m = 32
ew = n * m
eb = m
dw = m * n
db = n
total = ew + eb + dw + db
ratio = n / m
print(ew)
print(eb)
print(dw)
print(db)
print(total)
print(ratio)

traps: A wide bottleneck can copy the input. Low reconstruction loss does not prove a useful code. Always report bottleneck size and test reconstruction on held-out data.
MSE and BCE are not interchangeable. Use MSE for real values and BCE for 0/1 pixels. Pair BCE with a sigmoid output so x-hat is a probability.
Compression ratio is not accuracy. A 31.25:1 ratio says the code is smaller; it does not say how much information survives.

Tied weights mean W_d = W_eᵀ, which is always possible since W_e is m×n and W_eᵀ is n×m. The two bias vectors b_e and b_d stay separate. Tied weights are optional, not a defining feature of autoencoders.
A linear autoencoder with squared error learns a PCA-like subspace, not necessarily the PCA eigenvectors. Any basis of the same subspace gives the same reconstruction error.

quiz.q: Define the encoder and decoder in an autoencoder.
quiz.a: The encoder q(z|x) maps input x to latent code z. The decoder p(x|z) maps z to reconstruction x-hat.

quiz.q: Why does an undercomplete bottleneck encourage useful features?
quiz.a: The code has fewer dimensions than the input, so the model cannot store every input value. It must keep shared structure that helps reconstruction, such as edges or shapes, and drop noise. This pressure is useful only when the code is narrow enough and the data has structure.

quiz.q: A 784-pixel input uses a 16-unit bottleneck. The encoder has a 784×16 weight matrix and 16 biases. The decoder has a 16×784 weight matrix and 784 biases. Find the total parameters and the compression ratio.
quiz.a: Encoder weights 784×16 = 12,544; encoder biases 16; encoder total 12,560. Decoder weights 16×784 = 12,544; decoder biases 784; decoder total 13,328. Total = 12,560 + 13,328 = 25,888 parameters. Compression ratio = 784/16 = 49:1.

quiz.q: A colleague reports 0.001 MSE with a 2,000-unit bottleneck for 1,000-pixel inputs. What is suspicious?
quiz.a: A 2,000-unit bottleneck for 1,000 pixels is overcomplete. The network can learn identity-like copying, so 0.001 MSE is weak evidence of useful features. Report loss on held-out data and test the code, for example by reconstruction after removing noise or by using z for a downstream task.

quiz.q: Compute binary cross-entropy for one pixel with x = 1 and x-hat = 0.9. Use natural log.
quiz.a: For x = 1 and x-hat = 0.9, L_BCE = −[1·log 0.9 + 0·log 0.1] = −log 0.9 = 0.1053 to 4 decimal places.

quiz.q: What does a denoising autoencoder add, and why?
quiz.a: It corrupts x to x~ and trains the decoder to output the clean x. The code must learn to remove noise, which gives more robust features and allows denoising at test time.

quiz.q: Why can a linear autoencoder with squared error be compared to PCA? What is not guaranteed?
quiz.a: A linear encoder and decoder with squared error learn the same m-dimensional subspace as PCA, because both minimize squared reconstruction error over an m-dimensional linear subspace. The individual weight columns are not guaranteed to be the PCA eigenvectors; only the subspace is matched.
L_sparse = L_reconstruction + λ Σⱼ |zⱼ|, where zⱼ is the j-th code unit and λ ≥ 0 sets the penalty strength.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, autoencoders are used for anomaly detection: train on normal data, flag inputs with high reconstruction error. Search for 'denoising autoencoder', 'sparse autoencoder', and 'PCA vs autoencoder'. Newer work uses masked autoencoders for self-supervised vision. The encoder-decoder pattern also appears in U-Net for medical images.
